title: Lost Ticket
statement: A ferry sold tickets numbered 0 to 1,000,000; every ticket was scanned at the gate except one. The scans arrive in random order on a device with almost no free memory. Find the unscanned ticket.
examples: Scans 3, 0, 1 for tickets 0 to 3: ticket 2 is missing

approaches.name: XOR every ticket number 0..n and every scan
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: Each scanned ticket cancels its own number; only the missing number is left, with no overflow risk.

approaches.name: Subtract the sum of the scans from n(n + 1) / 2
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Also correct, but the sum needs a 64-bit number for large n.

approaches.name: Put every scan in a set, then check 0..n
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but it needs memory for a million numbers, which the device does not have.

approaches.name: Report the scan that arrived last plus one
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Scans arrive in random order, so the last one says nothing about the missing ticket.

title: Feature Flags
statement: An app has 30 on/off features per user and must store millions of users' settings compactly, then check and change single features quickly.
examples: Turn on feature 5 for a user
constraints: 30 features per user; millions of users

approaches.name: One 32-bit number per user, one bit per feature
approaches.label: best
approaches.why: flags | (1 << i) turns a feature on, flags & ~(1 << i) turns it off, and (flags >> i) & 1 reads it.

approaches.name: An array of 30 booleans per user
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Simple and correct, but it uses many times more memory across millions of users.

approaches.name: A comma-separated string of the features that are on
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Every check and change has to parse and rebuild the string, and the size grows with the features turned on.

title: Prime Table
statement: A math game must answer "is this number prime?" for 100,000 questions about numbers below 10,000,000.

approaches.name: Build a sieve of Eratosthenes once, then look each answer up
approaches.hint: Prepare a table once, answer many times
approaches.label: best
approaches.time: O(n log log n) once, O(1) per question
approaches.why: One sieve pass marks every number below 10^7; each question is then a single array read.

approaches.name: For each question, try dividing by every number up to its square root
approaches.hint: Check one number at a time
approaches.label: valid
approaches.why: Correct, but about 3,000 divisions per question, 300 million in total.

approaches.name: Answer "prime" for every odd number
approaches.label: unsuitable
approaches.why: Many odd numbers, such as 9 and 15, are not prime.
